name: Kingdom of Mrauk U (Arakan)
summary: A coastal kingdom on the Bay of Bengal, mixing Buddhist kings with Muslim titles; rich from trade and slave raiding in Bengal, it was conquered by Burma’s Konbaung dynasty in 1785.

location.value: The Rakhine (Arakan) coast of western Myanmar on the Bay of Bengal, at times also ruling Chittagong in today’s Bangladesh.

terrain.value: A narrow coastal plain cut by tidal rivers and creeks, cut off from inland Burma by the Arakan Yoma mountains.

climate.value: Tropical monsoon: very heavy summer rains (often over 4,000 mm a year) and a dry season from November to April.

resources.value: Fertile rice land, fish, timber, salt and a good position for sea trade across the Bay of Bengal.

disasters.value: Cyclones and storm surges from the Bay of Bengal; floods in the monsoon; fires in the wooden capital.

population.value: Perhaps a few hundred thousand; European visitors in the 1600s described the capital as a crowded city of over 100,000.

urbanisation.value: Mrauk U itself was a walled city of canals, palaces and stone temples; Chittagong and Sandoway were ports.

disease.value: Malaria, cholera and smallpox, common on the humid Bay of Bengal coast.

migration.value: Raids on Bengal brought thousands of captives to Arakan; Muslim traders, Portuguese adventurers and Japanese Christian guards also settled.

economicBase.value: Rice farming, sea trade, and slaves taken in raids on Bengal and sold to Dutch and other traders.

tradeRoutes.value: Bay of Bengal sea routes linking Bengal, Burma, the Malay world and India; the Dutch East India Company traded there from the 1620s.

wealth.value: Richest in the 1600s from trade and raiding; temples and the palace were richly gilded.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver coins (tanka) with Arakanese, Persian and Bengali writing; land taxes in rice and customs on trade.

inequality.value: A court nobility and monks above farmers; captives from Bengal were often enslaved or settled as royal servants.

governmentType.value: A Buddhist monarchy whose kings also used Muslim-style titles, reflecting ties with the Bengal Sultanate.

keyRulers.value: Min Saw Mon (Narameikhla), founder (1429–33); Min Bin (1531–54), who built the great temples; Thiri Thudhamma (1622–38).

succession.value: Kings came from the royal family, but palace coups and murders were frequent.

institutions.value: A royal court with ministers and governors, the Buddhist monkhood (sangha), and Portuguese and Muslim officers in service.

stability.value: Strong in the 1500s–1600s; after the loss of Chittagong (1666) court soldiers made and unmade kings, and the kingdom weakened.

eliteConflict.value: Court factions and palace guards fought over the throne; after 1700 kings often reigned only a few years.

armyAndTech.value: A war fleet of oared boats, Portuguese mercenaries with firearms and cannons, and city walls built with earth and stone.

majorWars.value: Wars with Toungoo Burma (1580s–1600s); fights with the Portuguese at Syriam; lost Chittagong to the Mughals (1666); Konbaung conquest (1784–85).

territoryChange.value: Held Chittagong (1666 lost to the Mughals).

alliancesRivals.value: Began as a vassal of the Bengal Sultanate; rivals were the Toungoo Burmese, the Mughals and Portuguese freebooters.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; skilled stone temple building and shipbuilding.

scienceEducation.value: Monastery schools taught reading and Buddhist texts; the court also patronised Bengali poets such as Daulat Qazi and Alaol.

openness.value: Very open: Muslim, Portuguese, Dutch and Japanese traders and soldiers lived at the capital.

communicationTransport.value: Boats on rivers, creeks and canals; sea ships along the coast; mountain passes into Burma.

religion.value: Theravada Buddhism was the state religion; a large Muslim community lived at the court and in the north.

languageWriting.value: Arakanese (Rakhine), written in Burmese-type script; Persian and Bengali were also used at court.

artsArchitecture.value: Fortress-like stone temples such as Shite-thaung (1535) and Koe-thaung (1550s), with thousands of carved Buddha images.

socialStructure.value: King and royal family, nobles and officials, monks, merchants, farmers, and captives or slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Rakhine (Arakanese) identity, centred on Buddhism and the Mahamuni Buddha image.

dailyLife.value: Most people farmed rice and fished; houses were of wood and bamboo on stilts; monasteries were the centre of village life.

neighbours.value: Bengal (and later the Mughals) to the north-west, Burmese kingdoms to the east, and the Bay of Bengal.

ideasReligions.value: Buddhist kingship mixed with Islamic court customs; Bengali Muslim literature flourished under Buddhist kings.

colonisation.value: Conquered by Konbaung Burma (1785), which took the Mahamuni Buddha to Amarapura; under British rule from 1826.

riseSignals.value: Min Saw Mon returned from exile in Bengal with Bengal Sultanate help and founded Mrauk U (1429–30).

peakPeriod.value: About 1530–1630, when Arakan held Chittagong and dominated the Bay of Bengal coast.

declineSignals.value: Mughal capture of Chittagong (1666) and long court instability after the killing of Shah Shuja (1661).

outcome.value: Conquered by King Bodawpaya of Burma (1784–85); the land became part of Burma, now Myanmar’s Rakhine State.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are well documented; population figures are estimates.
